title: Acquire Infrastructure
summary: Acquire Infrastructure covers the resource acquisition that happens before and around targeting, which is why it sits in the resource development tactic rather than in the intrusion itself. The adversary buys, rents, or otherwise obtains servers, domains, certificates, and third-party web services, and those assets become the staging points, redirectors, and command endpoints used later. Two properties make this effective. First, the acquired resources are ordinary commercial services, so traffic to them resembles normal business traffic and reputation-based blocking is weak. Second, they can be provisioned and discarded quickly, so the infrastructure an investigation eventually identifies may already be abandoned. Providers that offer free trial capacity and services that rent access to already infected hosts lower the cost and the barrier. Because this activity occurs outside the victim estate, most of the evidence is not in the victim logs at all; defenders observe the consequences at the network edge, in the form of newly registered domains, hosting address ranges with no established reputation, proxy or residential exit nodes, and authentication or traffic patterns that are inconsistent with the claimed client. Correlating that behaviour with threat intelligence about infrastructure age and reuse is the practical countermeasure, and defensive success is measured by how quickly hostile infrastructure is identified and filtered.

beginner.definition: This technique is about attackers obtaining the equipment they need before an attack. They buy or rent servers, register internet names called domains, and use rented online services. These assets host their tools and receive the results. The attacker rarely owns them for long.
beginner.whyItMatters: Attackers who use normal rented services blend in with everyday internet traffic. Blocking by name or address is hard, because the addresses are legitimate and change often. They can also abandon the resources quickly, so a block may arrive too late. This makes it difficult to trace activity back to a person. No single alert tells you an attacker is preparing, so behaviour and reputation are your best signals.
howItWorks: The attacker chooses services that suit the plan, such as cloud servers or web hosting.
They pay for them, often with a card or account that is hard to trace.
They register domain names and point them at those servers.
They may rent access to networks of already infected computers.
They configure the assets as relay points so victim traffic hides behind them.
After use they shut the assets down and obtain new ones for the next attempt.
beginner.example: Think of a burglar who rents a plain van and a storage unit. The van and the unit are legal and look ordinary on any street. Nobody can trace them to the burglar just by looking. When the job is finished, the van goes back and the unit is emptied.
takeaways: Judge internet traffic by behaviour and reputation, not just by address.
Track the age of domains and certificates you see in your logs.
Log authentication details that help separate real users from proxies.

objectives: Describe the kinds of infrastructure attackers buy or rent for operations.
Explain why commercial, rapidly replaced assets are hard to block.
Recognise network indicators such as new domains and unusual hosting ranges.
Explain why this activity mostly appears outside victim log sources.
Outline how threat intelligence supports filtering hostile infrastructure.
